transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump says everything's going good,
as midterm elections that'll serve as a referendum on his second term come to a close.
Americans angry over high prices and the Iran war are deciding whether to shift power in Washington.
Democrats are cautiously optimistic.
They hope discontent over Trump's handling of the economy will depress Republican turnout.
Trump said on Fox News this morning that inflation is solved.
The Commerce Department says consumer prices rose 3.6 percent in September from a year earlier.
Polls are still open across the country with control of Congress at stake.
And Piers Domenico Montanaro reports turnout is expected to be high.
It's election day and more than 59 million people have already voted.
That's a record for a midterm and is nearly half the entire 2022 midterm election.
Turnout experts believe it's possible this year could be a record-breaking year for a midterm.
Democrats lead in early voting by double digits,
but it's hard to read too much into that because Republicans vote overwhelmingly in person on election day.
Results will begin coming in during the 6 o'clock Eastern Time Hour and continue through midnight or later.
Many races will not be called by the time most people go to bed on the East Coast,
something that's normal and happens in every U.S. election.
Patience is going to be key as tens of millions of more Americans are expected to vote today.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
One state that could determine control of the U.S. Senate is Michigan.
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed is the Democrat running against Republican former Congressman Mike Rogers,
and Piers Sam Greenglass has more on the race.
Michigan is one of only two states.
President Trump won in 2024, where Democrats are defending a Senate seat.
El-Sayed is running to push Medicare for all and curb special interest money in politics.
Has Donald Trump done a good job keeping costs down?
And they got nothing to say about how they're going to fix that.
Their whole campaign has been to point to me and talk about my name and my faith.
Rogers' closing argument has focused on painting El-Sayed as dangerous.
This is how we get it done. Faith, family, and freedom.
We will be the ones that defend America for the next generation.
A third of Michigan-registered active voters submitted ballots before Election Day polls opened this morning.
Sam Greenglass, NPR News, Detroit.
President Trump told Fox News this morning that the U.S. military conducted strikes on some Iranian targets overnight,
saying, "It's just a minor attack. It wasn't war."
Iranian state television earlier reported that explosions were heard on Keshum Island.
The strikes in the Strait of Hormuz are raising more questions about what's coming next.
For weeks, Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
Meanwhile, Trump says the U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027,
but he says the U.S. will still sell arms to Israel.
U.S. stocks closed up today. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Massive flooding in the southwestern U.S. has turned communities into lakes of mud with residents starting cleanup efforts.
In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, the San Juan River caused severe flooding.
Some communities in Colorado and Utah made alternative voting plans.
The skies are clearing in the Four Corners area, and hundreds of evacuees are returning home, but the risk of flooding remains.
When results start coming in tonight, NPR will be relying on race calls from the Associated Press.
NPR's Tamara Keith explains how they do it.
AP will have more than 5,000 journalists working before and after polls close, gathering election returns from every state, county, city and township.
We like to brag and call it the single biggest act of journalism there is for a single story.
David Scott runs AP Elections, and he says there's a reason they call it a race call and not a projection.
The certainty required for us is that word. It's certainty.
We are certain, based on all the data, on all the evidence that we are looking at, that the trailing candidates can't catch up.
That means AP's calls sometimes come in more slowly than network TV projections.
Better to be sure than to be first.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
Five people, including two children, have been rescued near the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff.
Four others are still missing. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports that villagers rescued the group Sunday after they had drifted more than 3,300 miles east from where they set off in Micronesia.
The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam says the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after they failed to return on July 30th. It's NPR.

topics.text: President Trump says everything is going good as midterm elections come to a close
Consumer prices rose 3.6 percent in September from a year earlier, Commerce Department says
Record early midterm voting, with over 59 million ballots cast before Election Day
Michigan Senate race: Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers as Democrats defend the seat
Trump says U.S. military conducted minor overnight strikes on Iranian targets near Keshum Island
Trump says U.S. will stop providing $4 billion yearly aid to Israel starting in 2027
Massive flooding in Pagosa Springs, Colorado and the Four Corners area forces evacuations and cleanup
AP explains how it makes race calls for election results
Five rescued after three months adrift in skiff near Kiribati; four still missing
